subject: design-technology
title: Stretch: Seasoning, Grain and Sustainable Sourcing
welcome_lead: Look closer at the rings, the kiln and the FSC stamp behind every responsible timber product.
meta_desc: Stretch into seasoning, grain direction and sustainable timber sourcing for GCSE D&T.
final_note: You can explain seasoning, grain direction and the FSC scheme.

walkthroughs.body_html: Freshly cut green timber can be 50% water by mass. As it dries it shrinks and may twist. Seasoning reduces moisture to about 10–15% so the wood is stable indoors before being made into furniture.

Kiln seasoning takes days but uses energy. Natural seasoning takes a year per 25 mm of thickness but uses only air. Kiln-dried timber is more consistent; air-dried is gentler on the grain and preferred by some craft makers.

walkthroughs.h2: FSC sourcing in a school project
walkthroughs.body_html: A school workshop buys oak with the FSC stamp. The Council certifies that the wood came from a forest replanted to keep growing — a clear way to evidence sustainability in a GCSE design folder.

mcqs.q: Why is injection moulding suited to high-volume production?
options: It is the cheapest method for any quantity.
It stays constant.

mcqs.q: Why do designers often use 5th to 95th percentile data instead of just the 50th?
options: Because law requires it.
It is the only way to make plastic items.
To accommodate the majority of users rather than just the average.
Because the 50th percentile is too unreliable.
